questions.question: Count the sigma and pi bonds in one molecule of a diene whose structure is shown.
questions.answer: C: 9 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds
steps: The diene is buta-1,3-diene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2, with 4 carbons and 6 hydrogens.
Sigma bonds: 6 C-H + 3 C-C (the two C=C each contain one sigma bond, plus the single C-C) = 9.
Pi bonds: one in each C=C double bond = 2.
So 9 sigma and 2 pi, option C.

questions.question: Name the product of an alkene (drawn) reacting with chlorine gas from four options.
steps: The alkene is 4-methylpent-1-ene: CH2=CH-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3.
Chlorine adds across the C=C, one Cl on each of C1 and C2: CH2Cl-CHCl-CH2-CH(CH3)2.
Name the chain as pentane with Cl on carbons 1 and 2 and a methyl on carbon 4: 1,2-dichloro-4-methylpentane (option D).

questions.question: State what a shown curly arrow represents: single electron or electron pair, forming radicals or ions.
questions.answer: D: a pair of electrons from a bond to an atom, forming ions
steps: A curly arrow with a full arrowhead shows the movement of an electron pair.
Here the pair in the C-Cl bond moves to the Cl atom, giving Cl- and a carbocation (heterolytic fission), so ions are formed.
Free radicals would need single-barbed half-arrows, one electron each.

questions.question: Give the systematic name of compound X, a chlorobutene drawn in a structure not present in the text.
steps: Compound X is CH3-CH=C(Cl)-CH3: the chlorine is on the carbon with the C=C that has the methyl group, so it is 2-chlorobut-2-ene (numbered so the Cl gets the lower locant).
On the Cl-bearing carbon, Cl has the higher priority than CH3; on the other carbon, CH3 has the higher priority than H.
In the drawing the Cl points up and the CH3 on the other carbon points down, so the higher priority groups are on opposite sides: E.
Name: E-2-chlorobut-2-ene (option A). Options C and D (3-chlorobut-2-ene) are not valid names.

questions.question: Identify the bonds broken and formed when ethene reacts with hydrogen over heated nickel to form ethane.
questions.answer: Broken: one C=C pi bond and one H-H sigma bond. Formed: two C-H sigma bonds.
steps: Ethene C2H4 + H2 gives ethane C2H6 over Ni.
The H-H bond breaks, so one H-H sigma bond is broken.
The C=C double bond loses its pi bond; the C-C sigma bond remains.
Ethane has 6 C-H bonds against 4 in ethene, so two new C-H sigma bonds form.

questions.question: Choose the major product of a reaction of an alkene shown as a diagram.
steps: The alkene is but-1-ene, CH2=CH-CH2CH3.
In electrophilic addition of HBr, H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (C1) and Br ends up on C2, via the more stable secondary carbocation (Markovnikov).
Major product: CH3-CHBr-CH2-CH3, 2-bromobutane, which is option A.
B is 1-bromobutane (minor), while C and D have five carbons so they cannot form.

questions.question: Cracking C10H22 gives two molecules of ethene and one hydrocarbon A. Find the formula of A.
steps: Each C2H4 accounts for 2 carbons and 4 hydrogens; two give C4H8.
Subtract from the alkane: C10H22 - C4H8 = C6H14.
Check: C6H14 + 2C2H4 = C10H22, so the atoms balance.
C6H14 is option B.

questions.question: Explain why 2-bromopropane forms in higher percentage than 1-bromopropane when HBr reacts with propene.
questions.answer: D: a secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary carbocation
steps: HBr adds by electrophilic addition via a carbocation intermediate.
Propene gives a secondary carbocation (CH3CH+CH3) or a primary one (CH3CH2CH2+).
Alkyl groups donate electron density (inductive effect), stabilising the secondary ion more.
The more stable secondary carbocation forms preferentially, giving 2-bromopropane.

questions.question: But-2-ene shows geometric isomerism. Which prefixes could be used in naming the isomer drawn, with both CH3 groups on the same side of the C=C? Options: A cis and E, B cis and Z, C trans and E, D trans and Z.
steps: The drawn isomer has both CH3 groups on the same side of the C=C (both at the bottom).
Same side means cis in the cis/trans system.
On each carbon the CH3 group has higher priority than H, so the two higher-priority groups are on the same side: Z.
So the prefixes are cis and Z, option B.

questions.question: Name the type of reaction when zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution to form copper.
steps: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from its salt.
Zn + CuSO4 gives ZnSO4 + Cu.
This is not addition, neutralisation or substitution in the sense of the options.
So the answer is B, displacement.

questions.question: Choose the ionic half-equation for a process occurring in the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction.
steps: Zinc atoms lose electrons to form Zn2+ ions, which is oxidation.
Zn2+ carries a 2+ charge, so two electrons are released.
Option D balances charge: 0 on the left and 2+ + 2(-) = 0 on the right.
Option D is correct; C has the wrong charge and copper half-equations are reductions.

questions.question: Find the mass of cyclohexene from 12.5 g cyclohexanol at a 51.2 % yield (the yield is read from garbled text).
steps: Mr cyclohexanol C6H12O = 100.0; moles = 12.5 / 100 = 0.125 mol.
Mr cyclohexene C6H10 = 82.0; theoretical mass = 0.125 x 82.0 = 10.25 g.
Actual mass = 10.25 x 0.512 = 5.25 g (yield 51.2 %, read from garbled text).
This matches option A.

questions.question: Choose the option that is NOT a way of limiting global problems caused by polymer disposal.
steps: Developing biodegradable polymers reduces persistent waste (a valid method).
Removing toxic gases from incineration reduces pollution (valid).
Reusing polymer products reduces waste (valid).
Exporting waste only moves the problem elsewhere, so B is not a solution.

questions.question: Which skeletal formula is E-2-chlorobut-2-ene? Choose from the four structures A to D shown.
questions.answer: A: CH3-C(Cl)=CH-CH3 with Cl and the C4 methyl on opposite sides of the C=C
steps: Structure: C1H3-C2(Cl)=C3H-C4H3.
On C2, Cl has higher priority than CH3.
On C3, CH3 (C4) has higher priority than H.
E means the Cl and the C4 methyl are on opposite sides (trans) of the C=C.
Of the structures shown, A has Cl and the C4 methyl on opposite sides, so A is E. C has them on the same side (Z); B and D are 1-chlorobut-2-enes.

questions.question: State the total number of sigma bonds in Z-2-chlorobut-2-ene.
steps: Formula C4H7Cl; the structure is CH3-CCl=CH-CH3.
C-H bonds: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7 sigma bonds.
C-C sigma bonds: 3 (C1-C2, C2=C3 sigma part, C3-C4); C-Cl sigma bond: 1.
Total sigma = 7 + 3 + 1 = 11 (option D). Each double bond contributes one sigma bond.

questions.question: Choose the systematic name of a compound whose structure is shown.
steps: The longest chain containing the C=C has six carbons, so the parent is hexene; numbering from the end nearer the double bond makes it hex-1-ene.
There are methyl groups on C4 and C5, so the locants are 4,5.
Name: 4,5-dimethylhex-1-ene (option C).

questions.question: Choose the structure named E-2-bromo-3-chloropent-2-ene from structure options.
steps: Draw CH3-C(Br)=C(Cl)-CH2CH3 (2-bromo-3-chloropent-2-ene).
Priorities: on C2, Br > CH3; on C3, Cl > CH2CH3.
E means the two higher priority atoms (Br and Cl) are on opposite sides of the C=C. In structure A Br points up and Cl points down, so it is E.
B has Br and Cl on the same side (Z). C is 3-bromo-2-chloropent-2-ene. D has Br on an sp3 carbon (not a 2-ene at that position).

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for a compound whose structure is shown.
steps: The compound is CH3-CH=C(Cl)-CH3, 2-chlorobut-2-ene.
On the Cl-bearing carbon, Cl has priority over CH3; on the other carbon, CH3 has priority over H.
In the drawing the Cl is at the bottom right and the higher priority CH3 is at the top left, so they are on opposite sides: E.
IUPAC uses E/Z for this, rather than cis/trans, so the answer is option C.

questions.question: Hydrocarbon X has molar mass 98 g mol-1 and does not decolourise bromine water. Choose its structure.
questions.answer: D: the 1,1-dimethylcyclopentane structure (a saturated C7H14 ring)
steps: No colour change with bromine water means there is no C=C, so X is saturated.
A (heptane, 100) and B (octane, 114) have the wrong molar masses.
C is a heptene, which has the right mass but would decolourise bromine water. D is a cyclopentane ring with two methyl groups, C7H14 with no C=C.

questions.question: Choose the most likely step in the reaction of propene with HCl.
questions.answer: C: the chloride ion attacking the secondary carbocation
steps: In electrophilic addition, H+ adds to the CH2 end of propene, giving the more stable secondary carbocation CH3-CH+-CH3.
Cl- then uses a lone pair to bond to the C+, so the curly arrow goes from Cl- to the positive carbon.
A shows the primary carbocation (less stable); B and D draw the arrow in the wrong direction (away from C+).
So C is the most likely step.

questions.question: Name the type of reaction of propene with HCl.
steps: Propene C=C adds HCl across the double bond.
Two atoms add to C=C with no atoms lost, so it is an addition.
The H+ from HCl is the electrophile, attacked by the pi electrons.
So it is electrophilic addition, option D.

questions.question: State the number of pi and sigma bonds in a cyclic hydrocarbon whose structure is shown.
questions.answer: A: 2 pi bonds and 11 sigma bonds
steps: The ring is cyclopenta-1,3-diene, C5H6, with two C=C double bonds.
Pi bonds: one in each C=C, so 2.
Sigma bonds: 5 C-C (ring, including the sigma bond in each C=C) + 6 C-H = 11.
So 2 pi and 11 sigma, option A.

questions.question: Choose the IUPAC name for a bromoalkene shown as a structure.
steps: Structure: BrCH=C(CH3)CH2CH3. The longest chain through the C=C is four carbons (butene), with the double bond at C1.
Br is on C1 and a methyl is on C2, so the name is 1-bromo-2-methylbut-1-ene.
Priorities: on C1, Br > H; on C2, CH2CH3 > CH3.
Br points up and the ethyl group points down, on opposite sides, so the isomer is E.

questions.question: Which molecule can exist as E-Z isomers: 2-chloro-4-ethylhex-3-ene, 3-chloro-2-methylhex-2-ene, 2,3-dimethylhex-2-ene or 2,5-dichlorohex-3-ene?
steps: E-Z isomerism needs each C of the C=C to carry two different groups.
A: C4 carries two identical ethyl-type groups (C5 chain and the 4-ethyl), so no E-Z.
B and C: C2 carries two CH3 groups, so no E-Z.
D: C3 has H and C2; C4 has H and C5, so both carbons differ and E-Z isomers exist.

questions.question: Name the monomer that forms a polymer whose repeat unit is shown.
steps: The repeat unit has two backbone carbons: one carries two CH3 groups, the other carries H and CH3
Closing the two chain bonds into a C=C gives the monomer (CH3)2C=CH(CH3)
The longest chain containing the C=C has four carbons, with the double bond at C2 and a methyl on C2, so the systematic name is 2-methylbut-2-ene
The other options are not correct IUPAC names for this compound (trimethylethene and dimethylpropene are not systematic, and 3-methylbut-2-ene numbers the chain wrongly)

questions.question: State the total number of sigma bonds in cyclohexa-1,4-diene.
steps: Cyclohexa-1,4-diene is C6H8 with a six-carbon ring containing two C=C bonds.
Ring C-C sigma bonds: 6 (each ring bond has one sigma bond).
C-H sigma bonds: 8.
Total sigma = 6 + 8 = 14, option D.

questions.question: Find the minimum volume of H2 at r.t.p. to reduce 1.60 g of cyclohexa-1,4-diene (Mr 80) to cyclohexane.
steps: Moles of diene = 1.60 / 80 = 0.0200 mol.
The diene has two C=C bonds, so it needs 2 H2 per molecule.
Volume = 0.0400 x 24.0 = 0.960 dm3, option C.

questions.question: Count how many of four statements about ethene reacting with acidified KMnO4 are correct.
steps: Product ethane-1,2-diol has no C=C, so no geometric isomerism: statement 1 is false.
The alkene is oxidised by KMnO4: statement 2 is true.
Bond angles fall from 120 degrees (sp2) to about 109.5 degrees (sp3): statement 3 is false.
Purple KMnO4 is decolourised: statement 4 is true. Two correct, option B.

questions.question: Choose the option that is not a chemical reaction: cracking, fractional distillation, polymerisation or reforming.
steps: Cracking breaks C-C bonds to form new molecules: chemical.
Polymerisation forms new covalent bonds: chemical.
Reforming changes the structure of alkanes into branched or aromatic compounds: chemical.
Fractional distillation only separates mixtures by boiling point: physical, so B.

questions.question: State the type of bond broken in ethene and the type of fission when ethene reacts with bromine.
questions.answer: Pi (C=C) bond broken by heterolytic fission
steps: Ethene adds Br2 to give 1,2-dibromoethane.
The bond broken in the ethene molecule is the C=C pi bond.
In electrophilic addition the pi electron pair moves to one atom, so fission is heterolytic.
Answer: pi bond, heterolytic fission.

questions.question: Choose the systematic name for a compound whose structure is shown (options: E/Z-5-methylhex-2-ene, E/Z-2-methylpent-4-ene).
steps: The longest chain containing the C=C has six carbons; numbering from the end nearer the double bond puts the C=C at C2 and the methyl branch at C5, so the name is 5-methylhex-2-ene
The names with pent-4-ene (options C and D) have the wrong chain length and numbering
At each end of the C=C one substituent is H and the other is a carbon chain; in the zigzag drawing the two chain carbons lie on opposite sides of the double bond
Higher-priority groups on opposite sides means E, so the compound is E-5-methylhex-2-ene

questions.question: State the general formula of cyclic alkenes such as cyclohexene.
steps: Cyclohexene is C6H10.
A ring adds one degree of unsaturation and the C=C adds another.
Acyclic alkenes are CnH2n; each ring lowers hydrogen count by 2.
So cyclic alkenes are CnH2n-2, option B.

questions.question: Choose the diagram showing two repeat units of the addition polymer of cyclohexene.
steps: In addition polymerisation the C=C opens, so the two ring carbons that were doubly bonded become part of the polymer backbone
Each repeat unit is therefore a cyclohexane ring joined to the chain through two adjacent (1,2) carbons
Only D shows each ring linked to the chain and to its neighbour through adjacent carbons; A is 1,3-linked, B is 1,4-linked and C joins the rings at a single shared carbon

questions.question: Find the mass of cyclohexanol needed to make 7.20 g of cyclohexene at 72.0 % yield (Mr 100.0 and 82.0).
steps: Moles cyclohexene = 7.20 / 82.0 = 0.08780 mol.
Moles cyclohexanol needed at 100 % = 0.08780 / 0.720 = 0.1220 mol.
Mass cyclohexanol = 0.1220 x 100.0 = 12.2 g.
This matches option D.

questions.question: Identify each double bond in a molecule with two double bonds, using options whose text is missing.
steps: The molecule is CH3-CH=C(CH3)-C(CH3)=CH-CH2CH3 (3,4-dimethylhepta-2,4-diene)
Double bond 1: on its CH carbon CH3 outranks H; on its other carbon the neighbouring C(CH3)= carbon outranks CH3; these two groups are on opposite sides in the zigzag, so E
Double bond 2: on its first carbon the C(CH3)= neighbour outranks CH3; on the CH carbon CH2CH3 outranks H; these are again on opposite sides, so E
Both double bonds are E, so the answer is A

questions.question: State the molecular formula of limonene.
steps: Limonene is a terpene with two C=C bonds and one ring.
Degrees of unsaturation = 3 (2 C=C + 1 ring).
So the formula is C10H16, option B.

questions.question: Find the empirical formula of the product when limonene is completely hydrogenated.
steps: Limonene C10H16 has two C=C bonds.
Complete hydrogenation adds 2 H2: C10H16 + 2H2 gives C10H20.
Empirical formula divides by the highest common factor 10: CH2.
So option D.

questions.question: Choose the statement about poly(ethene) that is NOT correct.
steps: Poly(ethene) is an addition polymer: statement A is correct.
Its repeat unit is CH2, so empirical formula CH2: statement D is correct.
Poly(ethene) is non-biodegradable: statement C is correct.
It has no C=C, so it does not decolourise bromine water: B is not correct.

questions.question: Find the percentage atom economy of making ethanol by fermentation of glucose: C6H12O6 gives 2C2H5OH + 2CO2.
steps: Mr glucose C6H12O6 = 180.
Desired product mass = 2 x 46.0 = 92.0 (2 C2H5OH).
Option D.

questions.question: Find the percentage atom economy of making ethanol by hydration of ethene: C2H4 + H2O gives C2H5OH.
steps: Addition reaction: all reactant atoms end up in ethanol.
Mr of product C2H5OH = 46.0.
Sum of reactant masses = 28.0 + 18.0 = 46.0.
Atom economy = 46.0 / 46.0 x 100 = 100 %, option D.

questions.question: State the numbers of pi and sigma bonds in beta-farnesene (C15H24).
questions.answer: B: 4 pi bonds and 38 sigma bonds
steps: Formula C15H24 has (2 x 15 + 2 - 24)/2 = 4 degrees of unsaturation.
beta-Farnesene is acyclic with four C=C bonds, so 4 pi bonds.
Atoms = 15 C + 24 H = 39; an acyclic molecule has 39 - 1 = 38 sigma bonds.
Total 4 pi and 38 sigma, option B (assumes the order pi then sigma as printed).

questions.question: Decide which of three formulae (i)-(iii) are correct for 1,4-diethylcyclohexene.
steps: (i) The skeletal formula shows a cyclohexene ring with an ethyl group on one carbon of the C=C (C1) and another on C4, which is 1,4-diethylcyclohexene
(ii) Counting atoms: 6 ring C + 2 x 2 ethyl C = 10 C; cyclohexene C6H10 loses 2 H and gains 2 C2H5, giving C10H18
(iii) The simplest whole-number ratio of C10H18 is C5H9, so the empirical formula is correct

questions.question: Choose which molecule has a geometric isomer from structure options.
steps: Geometric isomers need each carbon of the C=C to carry two different groups
In A, B and C one carbon of the C=C carries two identical CH3 groups, so no E/Z isomers exist
In D (CH3CH=CHCH2CH3) one carbon has H and CH3 and the other has H and CH2CH3, so it has E and Z forms

questions.question: Choose the correct mechanism for electrophilic addition of HBr to pent-1-ene giving the major product.
steps: Step 1: a curly arrow starts at the C=C and points to the H of the polarised H(delta+)-Br(delta-); a second arrow starts at the H-Br bond and points to Br
Step 2: the arrow from the lone pair on the bromide ion Br- must point to the C+ of the carbocation, and the ion carries a full negative charge, not delta-
A has the last arrow reversed, C has the first arrow reversed, and D shows Br with delta- instead of Br-; only B is fully correct

questions.question: State the molecular formula of naphthalene.
steps: Naphthalene is two fused benzene rings.
Each ring-fused carbon pair shares atoms; there are 10 carbons.
Degrees of unsaturation = 7 (2 rings + 5 C=C).

questions.question: Choose which structure is a Z-isomer.
steps: Z means the two higher-priority groups (by CIP rules) are on the same side of the C=C
A: Cl and CH3 are on opposite sides, so E
B: Cl (higher than OH) and ethyl (higher than methyl) are on opposite sides, so E
C: Br (higher than Cl) is up and Cl (higher than ethyl) is down, so E
D: Cl and ethyl are both on the upper side, so Z

questions.question: Choose the skeletal formula of the major product when bromine water reacts with 2-methylbut-2-ene.
steps: In bromine water the alkene attacks Br2, then water (the solvent) attacks the more stable carbon of the intermediate, so Br and OH end up on adjacent carbons
The more substituted (tertiary) carbon of 2-methylbut-2-ene bears the OH group, and Br goes on the CH carbon
This gives (CH3)2C(OH)-CHBr-CH3, shown in A; B has the groups the wrong way round and C and D have the wrong carbon skeleton

questions.question: Describe what is seen when bromine water is shaken with propane and with propene.
questions.answer: Propane: no change (stays orange-brown). Propene: decolourises to colourless.
steps: Propane is saturated, so it has no C=C to react with Br2.
Bromine water stays orange-brown with propane.
Propene adds Br2 across its C=C, which removes the bromine colour.
Propene turns from orange-brown to colourless.

questions.question: Give the reagents and conditions for converting ethene to ethanol.
questions.answer: Steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst at about 300 C and 60-70 atm.
steps: Ethene is hydrated by steam (H2O) in an addition reaction.
Catalyst: concentrated phosphoric acid on a solid support.
Conditions: about 300 C and 60-70 atm pressure.
High pressure favours the fewer-gas-molecules side; the catalyst gives a fast rate.

questions.question: Give the reagents and conditions for converting ethene to ethane-1,2-diol.
steps: Ethene is oxidised to a diol across the C=C.
Use cold dilute aqueous KMnO4 (alkaline).
Hot or concentrated conditions would break the C=C instead.
So cold dilute alkaline KMnO4.

questions.question: Draw the structure of Z-3-methylpent-2-ene.
questions.answer: CH3-CH=C(CH3)-CH2CH3 with the C1 CH3 and the ethyl group on the same side of the C=C.
steps: Chain: C1H3-C2H=C3(CH3)-C4H2-C5H3.
On C2 the higher priority group is CH3 (C1) rather than H.
On C3 the ethyl group (C4) has higher priority than the methyl branch.
Z means these two higher-priority groups are on the same side (cis).

questions.question: 720 cm3 H2 at r.t.p. reacts with 0.010 mol of an alkene to give an alkane. Find the number of C=C per molecule.
steps: Ratio H2 : alkene = 0.030 / 0.010 = 3.
Each C=C takes one H2, so 3 double bonds per molecule.
Answer: 3.

questions.question: Describe three changes to a student's mechanism for the addition of bromine to ethene.
questions.answer: (1) The first curly arrow must start at the C=C and end at the nearer Br, not the reverse; (2) the Br-Br dipole is swapped: the Br nearer the alkene is delta+ and the far Br delta-; (3) the bromide ion must be Br- (with a lone pair), not Br+
steps: Change 1: the first curly arrow points the wrong way; it must start at the C=C double bond (the electron-rich pi bond) and end at the Br atom nearer the alkene
Change 2: the dipole on bromine is reversed; the Br nearer the alkene must be delta+ and the far Br delta-; the arrow from the Br-Br bond to the far Br, which becomes Br-, is then correct
Change 3: in the second step the bromide ion is labelled Br+; it must be Br- (negative charge) with a lone pair, which attacks the C+
The carbocation intermediate and the final product, 1,2-dibromoethane, are otherwise correct

questions.question: Draw the monomer of a polymer whose section is shown.
steps: The repeat unit is -CH(CH3)-CH2-, with two backbone carbons
Reopen the repeat unit as a C=C to give the monomer
Draw the monomer as CH3-CH=CH2 (propene): one carbon carries CH3 and H, the other carries two H

questions.question: Give the empirical formula of 2-methylpropene (C4H8).
steps: Molecular formula of 2-methylpropene is C4H8.
Divide each subscript by the highest common factor 4.
C1H2 gives the empirical formula CH2.

questions.question: Give a reason why 2-methylpropene does not show geometric isomerism.
questions.answer: One carbon of the C=C has two identical CH3 groups.
steps: Geometric isomerism needs two different groups on each C of the C=C.
2-methylpropene is CH2=C(CH3)2.
The C(CH3)2 carbon carries two identical CH3 groups.
So the two sides are not different and no E/Z isomers exist.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for 2-methylpropene reacting with Br2, including curly arrows, lone pairs and dipoles.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition via a tertiary carbocation giving 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane.
steps: Br2 is non-polar but is polarised by the approach of the C=C (induced dipole).
The C=C pi electrons attack the delta+ Br, with an arrow from C=C to Br.
The Br-Br bond breaks heterolytically; the bromide ion takes the bonding pair (arrow to Br-).
The tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C+-CH2Br is attacked by Br- (lone pair arrow), giving (CH3)2CBr-CH2Br.

questions.question: Give the skeletal formula of the organic product Q from Reaction 1 (2-methylpropene with acidified KMnO4).
questions.answer: 2-methylpropane-1,2-diol: skeletal formula with a carbon carrying two CH3 groups and an OH, joined to a CH2OH
steps: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the C=C of an alkene to a diol (OH added to each carbon of the double bond)
In 2-methylpropene (CH3)2C=CH2 one OH goes on the carbon with the two methyls and one on the CH2
Q is HOCH2-C(CH3)2-OH; draw a carbon with two methyl lines, an OH, and a CH2-OH branch

questions.question: Give the colour change seen during Reaction 1.
steps: Acidified KMnO4 contains Mn(VII) and is purple.
The alkene reduces it to Mn(II).
Mn(II) salts are almost colourless.
So the colour changes from purple to colourless.

questions.question: Identify reagent B in Reaction 2, which gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane as the major product.
steps: The product 2-bromo-2-methylpropane has Br added to the C=C.
Adding Br and H across C=C is HBr addition.
So reagent B is HBr (hydrogen bromide).

questions.question: Explain why 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is the major product of Reaction 2.
questions.answer: HBr adds via a tertiary carbocation, the most stable carbocation, because three alkyl groups donate electrons.
steps: HBr adds to 2-methylpropene by electrophilic addition via a carbocation.
H adds to the CH2, leaving a carbocation on the central carbon.
The central carbon has three alkyl groups, so it is a tertiary carbocation.
Alkyl groups donate electron density (inductive effect), stabilising it most; the major product is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

questions.question: Draw two repeat units of poly(2-methylpropene).
steps: Monomer CH2=C(CH3)2 opens its C=C.
Repeat unit is -CH2-C(CH3)2- (two carbons in the chain, two CH3 on one).
Join two units head to tail: -CH2-C(CH3)2-CH2-C(CH3)2-.
Chain ends are shown with bonds extending from the outer CH2 and C(CH3)2 groups.

questions.question: A 58.2 % yield reaction makes 2-methylpropene from 6.85 g of 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Find the mass of alkene formed.
steps: Mr 2-methylpropan-2-ol C4H10O = 74.0; moles = 6.85 / 74.0 = 0.0926 mol.
One mole of alcohol gives one mole of C4H8 (Mr 56.0) by dehydration.
Theoretical mass = 0.0926 x 56.0 = 5.18 g.
Actual mass = 5.18 x 0.582 = 3.02 g (3 significant figures, as for 6.85 and 58.2).

questions.question: Explain why coffee grounds might be considered a carbon-neutral fuel.
questions.answer: The plant material absorbed CO2 while growing, which is released on burning, so there is no net increase.
steps: Coffee grounds come from plants that take up CO2 by photosynthesis.
Burning them releases the same CO2 back.
So the net CO2 added to the atmosphere is about zero.
This is unlike fossil fuels, which release carbon stored for millions of years.

questions.question: Explain how using fossil fuels causes climate change.
questions.answer: Burning fossil fuels releases CO2, a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation and increases global temperature.
steps: Fossil fuels contain carbon stored for millions of years.
Combustion releases CO2 into the atmosphere, raising its concentration.
CO2 absorbs infrared radiation emitted from Earth's surface.
This enhanced greenhouse effect warms the atmosphere and causes climate change.

questions.question: Name another pollutant formed by incomplete combustion of alkanes (besides soot).
steps: Incomplete combustion occurs with limited oxygen.
Carbon is only partly oxidised.
Carbon monoxide is formed alongside soot.
So the pollutant is carbon monoxide.

questions.question: Write the equation for the complete combustion of octane (no state symbols required).
steps: Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O only.
C8H18 gives 8 CO2 and 9 H2O.
Oxygen atoms on the right: 16 + 9 = 25, so 12.5 O2 are needed.
Doubling gives whole numbers: 2C8H18 + 25O2 -> 16CO2 + 18H2O.

questions.question: Name the process that converts long-chain alkanes into smaller alkenes and alkanes.
steps: Long alkanes are broken into smaller molecules.
Heat (thermal) or a catalyst is used.
Alkenes are produced alongside smaller alkanes.
The process is cracking.

questions.question: Give a test for alkenes, including the positive result.
questions.answer: Add bromine water: an alkene decolourises it from orange-brown to colourless.
steps: Add bromine water (or acidified KMnO4) to the sample and shake.
Alkenes have C=C, which add across Br2.
A positive result: orange-brown bromine water goes colourless.
With acidified KMnO4 the purple colour goes colourless.

questions.question: Write a balanced equation for the polymerisation of ethene using displayed formulae.
steps: Each ethene monomer has one C=C.
The C=C opens and each carbon bonds to the next monomer.
n monomers join to form a chain with n repeat units.
Equation: n(H2C=CH2) -> [-CH2-CH2-]n, with the displayed C=C opened.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using ripening bananas as a source of ethene for polymers.
questions.answer: Advantage: renewable, no fossil fuels. Disadvantage: only tiny amounts of ethene, so not practical on a large scale.
steps: Advantage: ethene from bananas is renewable and does not use crude oil.
Disadvantage: bananas release only very small amounts of ethene.
Collecting and concentrating it would be costly and impractical at scale.
So bananas are not a practical bulk source.

questions.question: State a hazard associated with hydrogen chloride released from burning poly(chloroethene).
questions.answer: It is corrosive and toxic, causing burns and respiratory irritation.
steps: HCl gas dissolves in moisture to form hydrochloric acid.
The acid is corrosive to skin and eyes.
Breathing HCl irritates and damages the respiratory system.
So HCl is corrosive and toxic.

questions.question: Suggest how hydrogen chloride can be removed from waste gases in an incinerator.
questions.answer: Pass the gases through an alkali solution (e.g. sodium hydroxide or calcium hydroxide) to neutralise the HCl.
steps: HCl is an acid gas.
Passing the waste gas through alkali neutralises it.
Example: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.
The solution is then discharged safely.

questions.question: Calculate the volume in cm3 of 0.0300 mol of cyclohexene (density 0.811 g cm-3).
steps: Volume = mass / density = 2.46 / 0.811 = 3.03 cm3.

questions.question: State the colour change when excess cyclohexene is added to liquid bromine.
steps: Liquid bromine is red-brown.
Cyclohexene adds Br2 across its C=C.
The bromine is used up, so the colour is lost.
Colour changes from red-brown to colourless.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for cyclohexene reacting with bromine, with curly arrows, dipoles and lone pairs.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: pi electrons attack delta+ Br, Br-Br breaks heterolytically, Br- attacks the carbocation to give 1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
steps: Br2 is polarised by the approaching C=C (induced dipole, Brdelta+ - Brdelta-).
The C=C pi electrons attack Brdelta+; arrow from C=C to Br.
Br-Br bond breaks heterolytically; arrow to the Br atom taking the bonding pair (Br-).
The cyclic carbocation (or bromonium ion) is attacked by Br- lone pair, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.

questions.question: State the meaning of ppm.
questions.answer: Parts per million: 1 ppm means 1 part of bromine vapour per million parts of air (by volume).
steps: ppm = parts per million.
For gases this is usually by volume.
1 ppm = 1 cm3 of bromine per 10^6 cm3 of air.

questions.question: 3.25 cm3 of bromine vapour leaks into a lab. Find the minimum lab volume so the concentration is at the safe level (1.1 ppm, the eye-irritation level).
steps: Safe concentration = 1.1 ppm = 1.1 cm3 of bromine per 10^6 cm3 of air.
Required air volume = 3.25 / (1.1 x 10^-6) = 2.95 x 10^6 cm3.
Assumes 1.1 ppm is the safe limit (the eye-irritation level).

questions.question: 0.0300 mol of cyclohexene reacts with exactly this amount of bromine. Find the minimum volume of water to dissolve it (bromine solubility 35 g dm-3, Br = 79.9).
steps: Cyclohexene reacts 1:1 with Br2, so moles Br2 = 0.0300 mol.
Volume = mass / concentration = 4.79 / 35 = 0.137 dm3.
So the minimum water volume is 0.137 dm3 (137 cm3).

questions.question: Write a balanced equation for the polymerisation of propene using displayed formulae.
steps: Propene is CH2=CH-CH3 with one C=C.
The C=C opens and monomers link head to tail.
Each repeat unit is -CH2-CH(CH3)-.
Write n monomers on the left and [-CH2-CH(CH3)-]n on the right.

questions.question: Give one difference between the polymerisation of propene and of lactic acid.
questions.answer: Lactic acid forms its polymer by condensation (losing water), while propene forms its polymer by addition with no small molecule lost.
steps: Propene polymerises by addition: all atoms stay in the polymer.
Lactic acid polymerises by condensation.
Condensation releases a small molecule, water.
So the key difference is that water is eliminated only in the lactic acid case.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term biodegradable.
questions.answer: Able to be broken down by microorganisms (or natural processes) into naturally occurring substances.
steps: Biodegradable materials are broken down by living organisms.
Microorganisms such as bacteria digest them.
Products are naturally occurring substances such as CO2, water and biomass.
So the material decays naturally over time.

questions.question: Give three advantages of biodegradable polymers.
questions.answer: Less landfill waste, less litter harming wildlife, made from renewable resources rather than crude oil.
steps: They break down, so waste does not accumulate in landfill.
They reduce litter and harm to wildlife in the environment.
They can be made from renewable feedstocks such as corn (lactic acid).
Less persistent pollution, so less need for incineration with toxic gases.

questions.question: State why isoprene does not have geometric isomers.
questions.answer: At least one carbon of each C=C has two identical groups (two hydrogen atoms in CH2=).
steps: Isoprene is CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2.
The terminal CH2= carbons each carry two H atoms.
Two identical groups on one carbon mean no E/Z isomerism.
So isoprene has no geometric isomers.

questions.question: Draw the geometric isomer of a related molecule that shows geometric isomerism (the molecule is shown in the PDF).
questions.answer: The molecule whose geometric isomer must be drawn is missing from the page image: there is a blank gap between 'A related molecule does show geometric isomerism' and 'Draw the geometric isomer of this molecule'.

questions.question: Give a reason why a double bond may result in geometric isomerism.
questions.answer: The pi bond prevents rotation about the C=C, so groups are fixed on each side.
steps: A C=C contains a sigma and a pi bond.
The pi bond needs p orbitals to stay aligned.
Rotation about the C=C is therefore restricted.
Groups stay fixed either on the same side (cis) or opposite (trans).

questions.question: An alkene has molar mass 112 g mol-1. Deduce its molecular formula.
steps: Alkenes have general formula CnH2n with Mr = 14n.
Molecular formula is C8H16.

questions.question: Draw the branched-chain alkene with molecular formula C4H8.
steps: C4H8 alkenes: but-1-ene, cis/trans but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene.
A branched chain means a CH3 branch on the main chain.
2-methylpropene is CH2=C(CH3)-CH3.
Drawn as a skeletal formula with C=C at one end and a branch at C2.

questions.question: Give the structures and names of the two geometric isomers of C4H8.
steps: Geometric isomers need a C=C with two different groups on each carbon.
But-2-ene CH3-CH=CH-CH3 has CH3 and H on each carbon.
Cis (Z): both CH3 on the same side; trans (E): on opposite sides.
So the isomers are Z-but-2-ene (cis) and E-but-2-ene (trans).

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formula of compound X formed in Reaction 1 from 1-methylcyclohexene.
questions.answer: 1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane: a cyclohexane ring with Br on each of two adjacent carbons and a CH3 on one of them
steps: Bromine adds across the C=C of 1-methylcyclohexene (electrophilic addition)
Each carbon of the former double bond gains one Br
Skeletal formula: cyclohexane ring, Br on C1 (which also carries the CH3 group) and Br on the adjacent C2

questions.question: Give the reagent and condition needed for Reaction 2 from 1-methylcyclohexene.
questions.answer: Reagent: steam (water vapour); condition: phosphoric acid catalyst at about 300 C and 60-70 atm
steps: Reaction 2 adds H and OH across the C=C: hydration of the alkene to an alcohol
Reagent: steam, H2O(g)
Conditions: concentrated phosphoric acid (H3PO4) as catalyst, about 300 C and 60-70 atm (alternatively accept concentrated sulfuric acid followed by water)
OH goes on the carbon with the methyl group, giving the tertiary alcohol 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol shown

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for iodine monochloride reacting with propene, with curly arrows, lone pairs and the intermediate and product.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: I+ adds to CH2, giving the secondary carbocation CH3CH+CH2I, which Cl- attacks to give 1-iodo-2-chloropropane.
steps: ICl is polar: Cl is more electronegative, so Idelta+ - Cldelta-.
The C=C pi electrons attack Idelta+ (arrow from C=C to I).
I bonds to the terminal CH2, leaving a secondary carbocation CH3CH+CH2I.
Cl- lone pair attacks the carbocation (arrow from Cl- to C+), giving CH3CHClCH2I (1-iodo-2-chloropropane).

questions.question: Give the name of the monomer that forms a polymer whose two repeat units are shown.
steps: The repeat unit is -CH(CH3)-CH(C2H5)-, two backbone carbons
Reforming the C=C between them gives CH3-CH=CH-CH2CH3
The longest chain has five carbons with the double bond starting at C2, so the monomer is pent-2-ene

questions.question: 0.0100 mol of alkene reacts with 600 cm3 of H2 at 298 K and 1.24 x 10^5 Pa to form an alkane. Find the number of C=C per molecule.
steps: Convert: V = 600 cm3 = 6.00 x 10^-4 m3.
Each C=C takes one H2, so the alkene has 3 double bonds.

questions.question: Write an equation for the incomplete combustion of one mole of propene giving CO2, CO, carbon and water only. Include state symbols.
steps: Carbon balance: 3 C = 1 CO2 + 1 CO + 1 C.
Hydrogen balance: 6 H = 3 H2O.
Oxygen balance: 6 O = 2 (CO2) + 1 (CO) + 3 (H2O), so 3 O2.
Water is shown as gas at combustion temperature; the state of water depends on conditions.

questions.question: State one similarity and one difference when propene reacts with acidified KMnO4 and with bromine water.
questions.answer: Similarity: both decolourise and react with the C=C. Difference: KMnO4 oxidises to a diol (purple to colourless), Br2 adds across the C=C (orange to colourless).
steps: Both reagents react with the C=C of propene.
Both cause a colour change to colourless.
KMnO4 is an oxidation giving a diol, from purple to colourless.
Bromine water adds Br2 across the C=C, from orange-brown to colourless.

questions.question: Draw the structure of poly(propene) showing two repeat units.
questions.answer: ...-[CH(CH3)-CH2]-[CH(CH3)-CH2]-... (head to tail chain with CH3 on alternate carbons)
steps: Propene CH2=CH-CH3 opens its C=C.
Repeat unit is -CH2-CH(CH3)-.
Join two units: -CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)-.
CH3 groups sit on alternate carbons of the chain.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of bromine monochloride to show the dipole.
steps: Cl is more electronegative than Br.
Electrons in the Br-Cl bond are pulled towards Cl.
So Br is delta+ and Cl is delta-.
Show as Brdelta+-Cldelta- with the arrow pointing to Cl.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for propene reacting with BrCl to form 1-bromo-2-chloropropane.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: Br+ adds to the terminal CH2, then Cl- attacks the secondary carbocation to give 1-bromo-2-chloropropane.
steps: BrCl is polar: Brdelta+ - Cldelta-.
The C=C pi electrons attack Brdelta+ (arrow from C=C to Br).
Br bonds to C1, leaving a secondary carbocation on C2.
Cl- lone pair attacks C2+ (arrow), giving CH2BrCHClCH3.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for the formation of propan-2-ol from propene and steam with an acid catalyst, adding curly arrows and the species formed in the final step.
questions.answer: H+ adds to C1 giving the secondary carbocation; water attacks it; loss of H+ gives propan-2-ol and regenerates H+.
steps: H+ from the acid catalyst is the electrophile; the C=C pi electrons attack it (arrow from C=C to H).
H bonds to C1 giving the secondary carbocation CH3CH+CH3.
A water lone pair attacks C+ (arrow from O to C), forming protonated propan-2-ol.
Loss of H+ (arrow from O-H to base, e.g. H2O) gives propan-2-ol and regenerates the H+ catalyst.

questions.question: Suggest two properties that make squalane useful in cosmetics.
questions.answer: It is unreactive (saturated alkane, stable) and a liquid that spreads easily / is non-toxic.
steps: Squalane is a saturated alkane, so it does not react readily with skin.
It is a liquid at room temperature, so it spreads and feels smooth.
Alkanes are non-toxic and chemically stable.
So unreactivity and liquid spreadability are useful properties.

questions.question: Give the molecular formula of squalane, the saturated alkane made from squalene.
steps: Squalane is a saturated acyclic alkane with 30 carbons.
Alkane general formula CnH2n+2 with n = 30.
So C30H62.

questions.question: Name a suitable catalyst for the hydrogenation of squalene.
steps: Hydrogenation of C=C uses a heterogeneous metal catalyst.
Nickel is the standard choice for hydrogenation.
Platinum or palladium also catalyse it.
So nickel.

questions.question: Find the maximum permitted mass of catalyst in 50 g of squalane (limit 0.2 ppm by mass).
steps: 0.2 ppm = 0.2 parts per million by mass.
Mass of catalyst = 0.2 x 10^-6 x 50 g = 1.0 x 10^-5 g.
This is 0.01 mg.

questions.question: A reactor at 200 C contains 8500 mol of squalene and H2 at 4.0 x 10^5 Pa, needing 500 m3 of H2 for complete hydrogenation. Find the number of C=C per squalene molecule.
steps: Per squalene molecule: 5.09 x 10^4 / 8500 = 5.99 H2.
Each C=C takes one H2, so 6 C=C bonds.

questions.question: Write the equation, using molecular formulae, for the complete hydrogenation of squalene to squalane.
steps: Squalene C30H50 has 6 C=C bonds (6 DoU).
Each C=C takes one H2, so 6 H2 are needed.
Product squalane is C30H62.
Equation: C30H50 + 6H2 -> C30H62.

questions.question: Suggest a suitable technique to obtain squalene from shark liver oil.
steps: Shark liver oil is a mixture of liquids with different boiling points.
Squalene has a higher boiling point than many components.
Fractional distillation separates liquids by boiling point.
Reduced pressure avoids decomposition at high temperature.

questions.question: Calculate the minimum number of sharks needed to produce 2.8 million dm3 of squalene, given each liver yields 300 g and density 0.86 g cm-3.
steps: Volume 2.8 x 10^6 dm3 = 2.8 x 10^9 cm3.
Sharks = 2.41 x 10^9 / 300 = 8.0 x 10^6 (8.03 x 10^6 before rounding).
Answer: about 8.0 x 10^6 sharks.

questions.question: Calculate the land area in km2 needed to make 2500 tonnes of squalane from corn starch (23 % yield; 0.093 hectares per tonne of starch; 1 hectare = 0.01 km2).
steps: Starch needed = 2500 / 0.23 = 10 870 tonnes.
Land = 10 870 x 0.093 = 1011 hectares.

questions.question: Explain why beta-farnesene shows geometric isomerism and has only two geometric isomers.
questions.answer: Only the C6=C7 double bond has two different groups on each carbon; the other C=C bonds have two identical groups (terminal CH2 or two CH3).
steps: beta-Farnesene has four C=C bonds.
Terminal =CH2 groups have two identical H atoms, so no E/Z.
C10=C11 has two CH3 groups on C11, so no E/Z.
Only C6=C7 has different groups on both carbons, giving E and Z: two isomers.

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formula of the Z-isomer of E-beta-farnesene and give the reason for the name Z.
questions.answer: The Z-isomer has the higher-priority chain groups on the same side of C6=C7 (zusammen means together).
steps: Z comes from German zusammen (together).
On C6 the higher-priority group is the CH2 chain (C5); on C7 it is the CH2 chain (C8) rather than CH3.
In the Z-isomer C5 and C8 lie on the same side of the C=C.
The E-isomer has them on opposite sides.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term structural isomers.
questions.answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae (different arrangement of atoms).
steps: Isomers have the same molecular formula.
Structural isomers differ in the connectivity of their atoms.
So their bonds connect the atoms in a different order or branching.
Example: alpha- and beta-farnesene are both C15H24.

questions.question: State the number of geometric isomers of alpha-farnesene, given its structure (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH2C(CH3)=CHCH2CH=C(CH3)CH=CH2.
steps: (CH3)2C=CH: two CH3 on one carbon, no E/Z.
C(CH3)=CH within the chain: different groups on both carbons, E/Z possible.
CH=C(CH3)-CH=CH2: different groups on both carbons, E/Z possible; the terminal CH=CH2 gives none.
Two E/Z double bonds give 2^2 = 4 geometric isomers.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show another structural isomer of C15H24.
questions.answer: Add one C=C between two adjacent ring carbons that each still carry an H (for example the two CH2 carbons at the far left of the left-hand ring); this gives C15H24
steps: The partly drawn skeleton has 15 carbons in three fused rings plus four methyl groups, which is the saturated C15H26
C15H24 has one fewer H2, so it needs one C=C in addition to the three rings
Draw a double bond between any two neighbouring ring carbons that have hydrogens (not at the carbons already carrying four C-C bonds), giving a valid structural isomer of C15H24

questions.question: Describe how a sample of octadecane can be obtained from a mixture of alkanes.
questions.answer: Use fractional distillation and collect the fraction with the boiling range of octadecane (the high boiling point, long-chain fraction).
steps: Heat the mixture so it vaporises in a fractionating column.
The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.
Long-chain alkanes like octadecane have high boiling points and condense lower in the column.
Collect the fraction that boils at the boiling point of octadecane.

questions.question: Complete the cracking equation: C18H38 -> 2C4H8 + ?
steps: Atoms of carbon: 18 - 2 x 4 = 10.
Atoms of hydrogen: 38 - 2 x 8 = 22.
The other product has formula C10H22.
Full equation: C18H38 -> 2C4H8 + C10H22.

questions.question: Give the skeletal formulae of the other three alkene isomers of C4H8 apart from but-1-ene.
steps: Alkene isomers of C4H8: but-1-ene, but-2-ene (two geometric forms), 2-methylpropene.
Cis-but-2-ene: CH3 groups on the same side of C2=C3.
Trans-but-2-ene: CH3 groups on opposite sides.
2-methylpropene: CH2=C(CH3)-CH3.

questions.question: Give the name and structural formula of each product from the reactions of but-1-ene shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: 1: 1,2-dichlorobutane CH3CH2CHClCH2Cl; 2: butane CH3CH2CH2CH3; 3: butane-1,2-diol CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2OH; 4: butan-2-ol CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 (major)
steps: Cl2 adds across the C=C: CH3CH2CHCl-CH2Cl, 1,2-dichlorobutane
H2 with a nickel catalyst hydrogenates the C=C: butane
Acidified KMnO4 oxidises the C=C to a diol: CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2OH, butane-1,2-diol
Steam with an acid catalyst hydrates the C=C; the OH goes on the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov), giving butan-2-ol as the major product (butan-1-ol is minor)

questions.question: Draw the displayed formula of poly(but-1-ene) showing two repeat units.
steps: But-1-ene is CH2=CH-CH2CH3.
Repeat unit is -CH2-CH(CH2CH3)-.
Join two units head to tail.
Result: -CH2-CH(CH2CH3)-CH2-CH(CH2CH3)-.

questions.question: State one advantage and one disadvantage of incineration for disposing of polymers, other than climate effects.
questions.answer: Advantage: energy can be recovered as heat/electricity and waste volume is reduced. Disadvantage: toxic gases (e.g. HCl, dioxins) are released.
steps: Burning polymers releases heat that can be used for electricity.
Incineration greatly reduces the volume of waste.
Burning PVC and other polymers releases toxic gases such as HCl.
So incineration needs gas cleaning to avoid harmful emissions.

questions.question: 35.0 cm3 of butane is burned in 300 cm3 of oxygen (same conditions; water is liquid). Calculate the final total volume of gas.
steps: CO2 formed = 35.0 x 8/2 = 140 cm3; water is liquid so takes no gas volume.

questions.question: Explain the main hazard of using butane in a portable heater in an enclosed space.
questions.answer: Incomplete combustion produces toxic carbon monoxide, which is odourless and binds to haemoglobin.
steps: Limited oxygen in an enclosed space leads to incomplete combustion.
Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (CO).
CO is colourless and odourless and binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport.
So poisoning (and CO build-up) is the main hazard.

questions.question: Deduce the molecular formula of limonene.
steps: Limonene is a terpene with 10 carbon atoms.
It has two C=C bonds and one ring: 3 degrees of unsaturation.
So C10H16.

questions.question: State the colour change when a few drops of acidified KMnO4 are mixed with a sample of limonene.
steps: Limonene contains C=C bonds which are oxidised.
KMnO4 (Mn VII) is reduced to Mn(II).
Purple MnO4- is decolourised.
So from purple to colourless.

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formula of the organic product of limonene with excess acidified KMnO4.
questions.answer: The tetraol: cyclohexane ring with CH3 and OH on C1, OH on C2, and a C(CH3)(OH)CH2OH group on C4 (formula C10H20O4)
steps: Limonene has two C=C bonds: one in the ring and one in the isopropenyl side chain
Excess acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises both, adding an OH to each carbon of each double bond
Ring C=C becomes C(OH)(CH3)-CH(OH); side chain C(CH3)=CH2 becomes C(CH3)(OH)-CH2OH
The product therefore has four OH groups (a tetraol)

questions.question: Name the type of reaction that limonene undergoes in (b)(i).
steps: Limonene's C=C is oxidised by acidified KMnO4.
Oxidation involves an increase in oxidation number of carbon.
Permanganate is the oxidising agent.
So the reaction type is oxidation.

questions.question: On heating limonene forms two molecules of a smaller hydrocarbon Q, which polymerises to a polymer for car tyres. Draw the structure of Q.
steps: Limonene is C10H16; two molecules of Q give C5H8 each (C10H16 = 2 C5H8).
C5H8 with two C=C is 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene.
Polyisoprene is the polymer used in tyres.
So Q is isoprene: CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2.

questions.question: Give two ways chemists can help minimise problems caused by disposal of polymers.
questions.answer: Develop biodegradable polymers; design polymers that are easier to recycle or recover energy from.
steps: Develop biodegradable polymers that break down in the environment.
Design polymers that are easy to recycle (single type, labelled).
Develop catalysts or processes to recycle polymers back to monomers.
Any two of these.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using liquid CO2 rather than hexane to extract limonene (CO2 does not escape).
questions.answer: Advantage: CO2 evaporates and leaves no solvent residue, is non-flammable. Disadvantage: needs high pressure, so expensive equipment.
steps: CO2 leaves as gas, so no solvent residue remains in the product.
CO2 is non-toxic and non-flammable compared with hexane.
Liquid CO2 requires high pressure equipment, which is expensive.
So advantage: no residue; disadvantage: high pressure cost.

questions.question: Calculate the mass in kg of orange peel (1.63 % limonene by mass) needed to obtain 30 cm3 of limonene (density 0.841 g cm-3).
steps: Mass limonene = 30 x 0.841 = 25.23 g.
Convert: 1548 g = 1.55 kg.

questions.question: Name the process that forms the gases produced in landfill.
steps: Organic waste is buried with little oxygen.
Bacteria break down the organic matter without oxygen.
This produces methane and carbon dioxide.
The process is anaerobic decomposition.

questions.question: State the main environmental problem caused by landfill gases, identifying the gas or gases responsible.
questions.answer: Global warming (enhanced greenhouse effect), caused mainly by methane and carbon dioxide.
steps: Methane and CO2 are greenhouse gases.
They absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface.
This raises global temperatures.
So the problem is global warming, due to CH4 and CO2.

questions.question: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced in a year by a landfill of 90 000 tonnes, given 12.5 dm3 of gas per tonne per day and the gas composition table.
questions.answer: About 3.39 x 10^8 g of CO2 per year (339 tonnes)
steps: Gas per day = 12.5 dm3 x 90 000 = 1.125 x 10^6 dm3
CO2 is 45 % by volume: 0.45 x 1.125 x 10^6 = 5.06 x 10^5 dm3 per day
Moles per day = 506 250 / 24.0 = 21 094 mol; mass per day = 21 094 x 44.0 = 9.28 x 10^5 g
Mass per year = 9.28 x 10^5 x 365 = 3.39 x 10^8 g (about 339 tonnes)

questions.question: Suggest two advantages of incineration over landfill.
questions.answer: Incineration reduces waste volume greatly and can recover energy as heat or electricity; it avoids methane emissions from landfill.
steps: Incineration reduces the volume of waste by a large factor.
Heat from burning can generate electricity.
Landfill releases methane, which incineration avoids.
Any two of these advantages.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage of recycling compared with landfill and incineration.
questions.answer: Conserves natural resources and reduces the need for new raw materials.
steps: Recycling reuses existing materials.
This reduces the extraction of crude oil or minerals.
Less waste goes to landfill or incineration.
So recycling conserves resources.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for iso-octane.
steps: Iso-octane is C8H18 with three methyl branches.
Longest chain is pentane (5 C).
Methyl groups at C2, C2 and C4.
So 2,2,4-trimethylpentane.

questions.question: Name the industrial process used to convert octane into iso-octane by heating with a catalyst.
steps: Octane is converted to a branched isomer of the same formula.
This rearrangement is called isomerisation.
It is done with heat and a catalyst.
So isomerisation (catalytic reforming).

questions.question: Give a reason why petrol needs a high proportion of iso-octane.
questions.answer: Branched alkanes burn more smoothly and reduce engine knocking, giving a high octane rating.
steps: Straight-chain alkanes ignite prematurely in engines.
Branched alkanes like iso-octane resist this.
This reduces knocking and gives a high octane rating.
So petrol performs better in car engines.

questions.question: Draw skeletal formulae of four isomers of 2-methylpropene (C4H8), including only one that does not decolourise bromine water.
questions.answer: But-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene (all alkenes), and cyclobutane (no C=C, does not decolourise bromine water).
steps: Alkene isomers of C4H8: but-1-ene, cis and trans but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene.
Any three of these decolourise bromine water.
Cyclobutane has C4H8 with no C=C.
Cyclobutane does not decolourise bromine water, so it is the only non-decolourising isomer.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for the major product of 2-methylpropene reacting with HBr, with curly arrows, lone pairs and dipoles.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition via tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+, then Br- attack to give 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
steps: H-Br is polar: Hdelta+ - Brdelta-.
The C=C pi electrons attack Hdelta+ (arrow from C=C to H).
H bonds to the CH2, leaving the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+ (arrow from H-Br to Br-).
Br- lone pair attacks C+ (arrow), giving (CH3)3CBr.

questions.question: Give the reason why the product in (c)(i) is the major product.
questions.answer: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is most stable, because three alkyl groups donate electron density to the positive carbon.
steps: The reaction goes through a carbocation intermediate.
A tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups.
Alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge (inductive effect).
So this intermediate forms preferentially, giving the major product.

questions.question: Compound X contains 92.3 % C and 7.7 % H by mass. Calculate its empirical formula.
steps: Divide by the smaller value: C = 1.00, H = 1.00.
Ratio 1 : 1.
Empirical formula CH.

questions.question: A 0.267 g sample of X vaporises at 85.0 C and gives 98.0 cm3 of gas. Calculate its molar mass (pressure read as 104 kPa from garbled text).
steps: Pressure read from garbled text (104 kPa); confirm against the PDF if in doubt.

questions.question: Deduce the molecular formula of X from its empirical formula (CH) and molar mass (about 78).
steps: Empirical formula mass CH = 13.0.
Molecular formula C6H6 (benzene).

questions.question: Describe the covalent bond between a silicon atom and an oxygen atom in silicon dioxide, in terms of particles.
questions.answer: A shared pair of electrons is held between the Si and O nuclei by electrostatic attraction.
steps: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
The shared pair is attracted to the positive nuclei of both Si and O.
This electrostatic attraction holds the atoms together.
In SiO2 each Si forms four such bonds in a giant lattice.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the covalent bonding in CO2 and SiO2 in terms of orbital overlap.
questions.answer: Both have sigma bonds from head-on overlap. CO2 also has pi bonds from sideways 2p-2p overlap; SiO2 has weak or no pi overlap because Si 3p orbitals are larger and overlap poorly with O 2p.
steps: Both C=O and Si-O have a sigma bond from head-on overlap.
In CO2 the C 2p and O 2p orbitals are similar in size, giving strong sideways pi overlap (C=O double bonds).
In SiO2 the Si 3p and O 2p orbitals are different sizes, so pi overlap is poor.
So SiO2 is effectively single Si-O bonds (sigma) with little pi bonding.

questions.question: Explain the shape of the carbon dioxide molecule.
questions.answer: Linear (180 degrees): carbon has two C=O bonding regions and no lone pairs, which repel equally to be as far apart as possible.
steps: Carbon has four outer electrons and forms two C=O double bonds.
Each double bond counts as one electron domain (bonding region).
There are no lone pairs on carbon.
Two domains repel to 180 degrees, so the molecule is linear.

questions.question: Explain the polarity of the carbon-oxygen bond.
questions.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the bonding electrons are pulled towards O: Odelta- and Cdelta+.
steps: Oxygen has a higher electronegativity than carbon.
The bonding electron pair is drawn towards the oxygen atom.
Oxygen becomes delta-, carbon becomes delta+.
This creates a polar bond (a dipole).

questions.question: State whether the carbon dioxide molecule is polar and justify your answer.
questions.answer: Not polar: the two C=O bond dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel out in the symmetrical linear molecule.
steps: Each C=O bond is polar.
The molecule is linear and symmetrical.
The two equal dipoles point in opposite directions.
They cancel, so CO2 has no overall dipole.

questions.question: Using the structure of diamond, suggest how the structure of silicon dioxide is similar.
questions.answer: Both are giant covalent lattices in which each atom is bonded tetrahedrally to four neighbours.
steps: Diamond is a giant covalent lattice of carbon atoms.
Each C is bonded tetrahedrally to four other C atoms.
In SiO2 each Si is bonded to four O atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement.
So both are giant covalent tetrahedral networks.

questions.question: Give a possible reason why SiO2 has a lower melting temperature than diamond even though the Si-O bond is stronger than C-C.
questions.answer: Si atoms are larger than C, so Si-O bonds are longer and the giant lattice is less rigid overall (possibly polar Si-O character reducing lattice strength).
steps: Si is a larger atom than C, so Si-O bonds are longer than C-C bonds.
Longer bonds mean the atoms are further apart in the lattice.
The lattice is therefore less tightly held overall, despite stronger individual bonds.
This lowers the energy needed to melt SiO2 compared with diamond.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the electron density areas of the sigma and pi bonds in a C=C double bond, and label each bond.
questions.answer: Sigma: electron density along the C-C axis between the nuclei. Pi: two lobes of electron density above and below the plane of the C=C.
steps: The sigma bond is formed by head-on overlap of orbitals.
Its electron density lies along the internuclear axis.
The pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals.
Pi electron density is above and below the plane of the C=C atoms.

questions.question: In each box, draw the organic product of the reaction of propene with the reagents shown.
questions.answer: Steam + acid catalyst: propan-2-ol CH3CH(OH)CH3 (major); acidified manganate(VII): propane-1,2-diol CH3CH(OH)CH2OH; bromine: 1,2-dibromopropane CH3CHBrCH2Br
steps: Steam and an acid catalyst add H and OH across the C=C; by Markovnikov addition the OH goes on the middle carbon, giving propan-2-ol
Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the C=C to a diol, CH3-CH(OH)-CH2OH
Bromine adds across the C=C to give CH3-CHBr-CH2Br
Draw each as a full structure in its box, with all atoms and bonds shown

questions.question: Give the mechanism for propene reacting with HBr to form the major product.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition via the secondary carbocation CH3CH+CH3 giving 2-bromopropane.
steps: HBr is polar: Hdelta+ - Brdelta-.
The C=C pi electrons attack Hdelta+ (arrow from C=C to H).
H bonds to C1 giving the secondary carbocation CH3CH+CH3 (more stable than primary).
Br- lone pair attacks C+ (arrow), giving 2-bromopropane.

questions.question: Give the molecular formula of alpha-ocimene, which has three C=C bonds.
steps: Alpha-ocimene is an acyclic terpene with three C=C bonds.
Three degrees of unsaturation with no ring.
So C10H16.

questions.question: Circle the part of alpha-ocimene's skeletal formula that gives rise to its geometric isomerism.
questions.answer: Circle the middle C=C, the internal double bond between the C(CH3) carbon and the CH carbon next to it
steps: Geometric isomerism needs each carbon of the C=C to have two different groups
The terminal CH2=CH and CH2=C(CH3) bonds each have two H on one carbon, so they cannot show it
The internal C=C has CH3 and CH=CH2 on one carbon and H and CH2CH2- on the other, so the circle goes round this bond

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formula of the other geometric isomer of alpha-ocimene.
questions.answer: Redraw the molecule with the internal C=C having the vinyl group (CH=CH2) and the CH2CH2... chain on the same side (the Z isomer)
steps: The drawn molecule has these two groups on opposite sides (the E isomer)
Keep the skeleton CH2=CH-C(CH3)=CH-CH2-CH2-C(CH3)=CH2 the same
Swap the side of the chain on one carbon of the internal C=C so that the two higher-priority groups are on the same side, giving the Z isomer

questions.question: 0.050 mol alpha-ocimene reacts with 3.6 dm3 H2 (molar volume 24 dm3 mol-1) with a catalyst. Deduce the structure of the product.
steps: Ratio H2 : ocimene = 0.150 / 0.050 = 3.
Each C=C takes one H2, so all three C=C are hydrogenated.
Product C10H22: 3,7-dimethyloctane (the saturated alkane with the same carbon skeleton).

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formulae of the four structural isomers of straight-chain alkene X that are alkenes (ignoring geometric isomers).
steps: X is pent-2-ene, C5H10, a straight-chain alkene with the C=C at C2
The other C5H10 alkenes are pent-1-ene (CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3) and the three branched ones
The branched ones are 2-methylbut-1-ene CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3, 3-methylbut-1-ene CH2=CHCH(CH3)2 and 2-methylbut-2-ene (CH3)2C=CHCH3
Draw each as a skeletal formula (zigzag chain with the double bond marked)

questions.question: Explain why alkene X can exist as geometric isomers.
questions.answer: The C=C restricts rotation, and each carbon of the C=C carries two different groups (for example H and an alkyl group).
steps: The C=C double bond (pi bond) prevents free rotation.
The two groups on each carbon are fixed on either side of the double bond.
For X each carbon of the C=C carries two different groups.
So cis and trans (E and Z) isomers can exist.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for compound Y (structure shown in the PDF).
steps: The main chain has four carbons with the C=C between C2 and C3, so but-2-ene
One Cl on each carbon of the C=C (C2 and C3), so 2,3-dichloro
The two Cl atoms are on opposite sides, so the isomer is E (not Z)

questions.question: Comment on a student's statement that compound Y has polar bonds so it is a polar molecule.
questions.answer: The student is wrong: the C-Cl bonds are polar, but in Y the dipoles cancel, so the molecule is non-polar overall
steps: C-Cl bonds are polar because Cl is more electronegative than C, so the student is right that Y has polar bonds
In Y the two Cl atoms are on opposite sides of the C=C and the molecule is symmetrical
The two bond dipoles are equal and act in opposite directions, so they cancel
There is no net dipole, so Y is non-polar; polar bonds alone do not make a polar molecule

questions.question: Calculate the amount in mol of bisabolene in 5.51 g (Mr 204.0).
steps: Moles = mass / Mr = 5.51 / 204.0.
Give as 0.0270 mol.

questions.question: Calculate the moles of H2 that reacted with the bisabolene, using 1873 cm3 at 150 C and 152 000 Pa (R = 8.31).
steps: So 0.0810 mol H2 reacted.

questions.question: Deduce the number of C=C bonds in one molecule of bisabolene from your answers to (c)(i) and (c)(ii).
steps: Ratio H2 : bisabolene = 0.0810 / 0.02701 = 3.00.
Each C=C takes one H2.
So each bisabolene molecule has 3 C=C bonds.

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formula of the monomer of polyisoprene.
steps: The repeat unit of polyisoprene is -CH2-C(CH3)=CH-CH2-.
Removing the chain bonds gives the monomer.
Monomer: CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2.
This is isoprene.

questions.question: A sample of polyisoprene has relative molecular mass 50 250. Calculate the number of repeat units.
steps: Repeat unit C5H8 has Mr = 5 x 12.0 + 8 x 1.0 = 68.0.
Number of repeat units = 50 250 / 68.0 = 739.
Answer: about 739 repeat units.

questions.question: Incinerators used to dispose of polymer waste have a system to remove waste gases. Suggest why these systems contain solid calcium hydroxide and why it is finely powdered.
questions.answer: Calcium hydroxide is a base that neutralises acidic waste gases (such as HCl and SO2); the fine powder gives a large surface area so the reaction is faster
steps: Burning polymers can release acidic gases such as hydrogen chloride (from PVC) and sulfur dioxide
Calcium hydroxide is a base, so it neutralises these acidic gases and stops them reaching the atmosphere
A fine powder has a large surface area, so more gas molecules collide with it and the reaction is faster

questions.question: Identify the catalyst needed for Reaction 1 from propene.
steps: Reaction 1 is the hydrogenation of propene to propane with H2(g)
A finely divided nickel catalyst is used (platinum or palladium also work)

questions.question: Name product A from the propene reaction scheme.
steps: Chlorine adds across the C=C of propene
Each carbon of the double bond gains one Cl, giving CH3CHClCH2Cl
Numbering the three-carbon chain gives 1,2-dichloropropane

questions.question: Identify the substances needed for Reaction 2 from propene.
questions.answer: Steam (water vapour) and a phosphoric acid (H3PO4) catalyst
steps: Reaction 2 converts propene to propan-2-ol by adding H and OH across the C=C (hydration)
The reagent is steam, H2O(g)
The catalyst is phosphoric acid, H3PO4 (at about 300 C and 60-70 atm)

questions.question: Draw the displayed formula of product B from the propene reaction scheme.
questions.answer: Propane-1,2-diol, CH3-CH(OH)-CH2OH, drawn as a displayed formula with every bond shown
steps: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the C=C of propene to a diol
An OH is added to each carbon of the C=C, giving CH3-CH(OH)-CH2OH
Draw all C-H, C-C, C-O and O-H bonds: three carbons in a row, OH on carbon 1 and carbon 2, H atoms to complete four bonds on each carbon

questions.question: Write the equation for the addition polymerisation of propene.
steps: Propene has one C=C.
The C=C opens and monomers link head to tail.
Repeat unit -CH2-CH(CH3)-.
Equation: n CH2=CHCH3 -> [-CH2-CH(CH3)-]n.

questions.question: State two problems with the disposal of polymers such as poly(propene).
questions.answer: They are non-biodegradable, so they persist in landfill; incineration can release toxic gases.
steps: Poly(propene) does not biodegrade, so it accumulates in landfill.
It takes up large land areas and can persist for many years.
Burning it releases toxic gases such as CO and soot.
Any two of these problems.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for HBr reacting with 3-bromopropene to give 1,2-dibromopropane.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: H+ adds to CH2= terminal carbon, giving secondary carbocation CH3-CH+-CH2Br, then Br- attacks to form CH3CHBrCH2Br.
steps: HBr is polar: Hdelta+ - Brdelta-.
The C=C pi electrons attack Hdelta+ (arrow from C=C to H).
H bonds to C1 (the CH2=), leaving the secondary carbocation CH3-CH+-CH2Br.
Br- lone pair attacks C+ (arrow), giving 1,2-dibromopropane.

questions.question: Explain why 1,2-dibromopropane is the major product rather than 1,3-dibromopropane.
questions.answer: The secondary carbocation formed is more stable than the primary one that would give 1,3-dibromopropane.
steps: Adding H to C2 would give a primary carbocation at C1 (CH2+ next to CH2Br).
Adding H to C1 gives a secondary carbocation at C2.
The secondary carbocation is stabilised by two alkyl groups (inductive effect).
So the 1,2-product is formed in greater amount.

questions.question: State what is meant by a saturated hydrocarbon.
questions.answer: A hydrocarbon containing only single C-C bonds (no C=C), such as alkanes with formula CnH2n+2.
steps: Saturated means all bonds between carbon atoms are single.
Each carbon has the maximum number of hydrogen atoms.
Alkanes are saturated with general formula CnH2n+2.
No C=C bonds means no addition with bromine.

questions.question: Describe how the fractions in crude oil are separated during fractional distillation.
questions.answer: Crude oil is heated and vaporised; vapours rise a column that is hotter at the bottom, and each fraction condenses at its own boiling range.
steps: Crude oil is heated until it vaporises.
The vapour enters a fractionating column hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.
Each fraction condenses where its temperature is below its boiling point.
Fractions with lower boiling points (shorter chains) are collected higher up.

questions.question: An inhaler with 120 doses contains 1.55 g of butane. Calculate the volume in cm3 of propellant per dose at 25 C and 100 kPa (R = 8.31).
steps: Mr C4H10 = 58.0; moles of butane = 1.55 / 58.0 = 0.02672 mol.
Moles per dose = 0.02672 / 120 = 2.227 x 10^-4 mol.

questions.question: Write an equation for the complete combustion of octane, C8H18, including state symbols.
steps: Octane is a liquid at room temperature (l).
Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O.
C8H18 gives 8 CO2 and 9 H2O, needing 12.5 O2.
Doubling: 2C8H18(l) + 25O2(g) -> 16CO2(g) + 18H2O(l).

questions.question: Give two reasons why alternative fuels such as bioethanol are being developed to replace fuels from crude oil.
questions.answer: Crude oil is non-renewable and running out; burning fossil fuels adds CO2 that contributes to climate change.
steps: Crude oil reserves are finite and non-renewable.
Bioethanol comes from renewable plant material.
Burning fossil fuels adds CO2 and contributes to global warming.
Biofuels can be close to carbon-neutral.

questions.question: Name the process that converts straight-chain alkanes such as octane into branched-chain alkanes to improve petrol.
steps: The molecular formula stays the same (C8H18).
Only the carbon skeleton is rearranged.
This rearrangement is isomerisation.
Branching improves the octane rating.

questions.question: Give an equation using skeletal formulae for the conversion of octane into 2,5-dimethylhexane.
steps: Octane is CH3(CH2)6CH3.
2,5-dimethylhexane has a six-carbon chain with CH3 branches on C2 and C5.
Both are C8H18, so this is an isomerisation.
Equation: straight-chain octane -> 2,5-dimethylhexane (skeletal formulae).

questions.question: Give a reason why oxygen should be excluded during steam cracking.
questions.answer: To prevent the hydrocarbons burning (combustion) to CO2 and water, which would waste feedstock and could form explosive mixtures.
steps: At 850 C hydrocarbons would react with oxygen.
Oxygen would cause combustion rather than cracking.
This wastes hydrocarbon feedstock and forms CO2 and water.
Excluding oxygen keeps the cracking reaction going.

questions.question: State one use of ethene.
steps: Ethene is a major petrochemical feedstock.
It is polymerised to make poly(ethene) plastics.
It is also hydrated to make ethanol.
Any one of these uses.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for ethene reacting with hydrogen bromide to form bromoethane, including curly arrows, lone pairs and dipoles.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: H+ adds to ethene forming CH3CH2+, which is attacked by Br- to give bromoethane.
steps: HBr is polar: Hdelta+ - Brdelta-.
The C=C pi electrons attack Hdelta+ (arrow from C=C to H).
H bonds to one carbon, forming the ethyl carbocation CH3CH2+ (arrow from H-Br to Br-).
Br- lone pair attacks C+ (arrow), giving CH3CH2Br.

questions.question: On the structure of zingiberene, circle the 2-methyl group referred to in its IUPAC name.
questions.answer: Circle the CH3 group attached to the ring carbon at the lower right of the ring (the ring methyl), not the methyl groups on the side chain
steps: The ring is numbered as cyclohexa-1,3-diene: C1=C2 and C3=C4 are the double bonds, C5 carries the side chain and C6 is the CH2
The 2-methyl group is on C2, the ring carbon double-bonded to C1 and single-bonded to C3
In the drawing that is the ring carbon at the lower right, whose methyl line points out to the right

questions.question: Deduce the molecular formula of zingiberene, with IUPAC name 2-methyl-5-(6-methylhept-5-en-2-yl)cyclohexa-1,3-diene.
steps: Carbons: ring 6 + 2-methyl 1 + side chain 8 (heptenyl 7 + methyl 1) = 15.
Unsaturations: 1 ring + 2 C=C in ring + 1 C=C in side chain = 4.
So C15H24.

questions.question: Name the type and mechanism of the reaction of zingiberene with excess HBr.
steps: HBr is an electrophile (H+ source).
The C=C pi electrons attack H+.
A carbocation intermediate forms, then Br- attacks it.
So electrophilic addition.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for zingiberene reacting with one molecule of HBr, using the simplified part A structure.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: curly arrow from the C=C to the H of H(delta+)-Br(delta-); arrow from the H-Br bond to Br; tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C+-CH2-A plus :Br-; arrow from a lone pair on Br- to C+; product (CH3)2CBr-CH2-A
steps: Show HBr with dipoles H(delta+)-Br(delta-); the first curly arrow starts at the C=C and ends at the H
A second curly arrow starts at the H-Br bond and ends at Br, forming Br- (with a lone pair)
The H adds to the CH carbon, so the positive charge sits on the carbon with the two CH3 groups: the tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C+-CH2-A
A third curly arrow starts at a lone pair on Br- and ends at the C+, giving (CH3)2CBr-CH2-A, product I

questions.question: Explain by referring to the mechanism why product I is the major product.
questions.answer: Product I forms through a tertiary carbocation, which is more stable than the secondary carbocation that would lead to II, so it forms faster and is the major product
steps: Adding H to the CH carbon gives a tertiary carbocation with three alkyl groups on the positive carbon
Alkyl groups push electron density towards the C+ (positive inductive effect), stabilising it
Adding H to the other carbon would give a secondary carbocation, with only two alkyl groups, which is less stable
The more stable tertiary intermediate is formed preferentially, so I is the major product

questions.question: Identify the catalyst for hydrogenation of zingiberene with hydrogen gas.
steps: Hydrogenation of C=C uses a metal catalyst.
Nickel is the standard catalyst.
Platinum or palladium also work.
So nickel.

questions.question: 2.0 mol of zingiberene react completely with hydrogen at 150 C and a pressure of 120 kPa. Calculate the minimum volume of hydrogen needed under these conditions, stating your units. [pV = nRT, R = 8.31 J mol^-1 K^-1]
steps: Zingiberene has 3 C=C bonds (one in the chain, two in the ring) and the product is fully saturated, so 3 mol H2 react per mol

questions.question: Give the names of reagent W and catalyst X in the propene reactions.
questions.answer: Reagent W: hydrogen (H2); catalyst X: nickel (Ni)
steps: Propene becomes propane, so H2 has added across the C=C (hydrogenation)
W is hydrogen
Catalyst X is nickel (platinum or palladium are also acceptable)

questions.question: Draw the displayed formula of compound Y in the propene scheme.
questions.answer: Propane-1,2-diol drawn in full: CH3-CH(OH)-CH2OH with all bonds shown
steps: Acidified manganate(VII) oxidises the C=C of propene to a diol
Compound Y is propane-1,2-diol
Displayed formula: three carbons in a row, OH on the first and second carbons, and enough H atoms so each carbon has four bonds

questions.question: Draw the skeletal formula of the major product Z.
questions.answer: 2-chloropropane: a skeletal zigzag of three carbons with Cl on the middle carbon
steps: HCl adds across the C=C of propene by electrophilic addition
By Markovnikov's rule H goes on the carbon with more H, so Cl bonds to the middle carbon via the more stable secondary carbocation
Z is CH3-CHCl-CH3, drawn as a V shape with Cl on the centre carbon

questions.question: Complete the two-stage mechanism for ethene reacting with steam to form ethanol, adding curly arrows and the relevant dipole.
questions.answer: Stage 1: H+ adds to ethene giving CH3CH2+. Stage 2: water attacks the carbocation, then loss of H+ gives ethanol.
steps: H3O+ (or H+) is polar: Hdelta+ is the electrophile.
C=C pi electrons attack Hdelta+ (arrow from C=C to H), forming CH3CH2+.
A water lone pair attacks the carbocation (arrow from O to C+), forming CH3CH2OH2+.
Water removes H+ from the oxonium ion (arrow from O-H to base), giving ethanol and regenerating H+.

questions.question: Predict the shape of the intermediate ion with reference to its positively charged carbon, and justify.
questions.answer: Trigonal planar around the positive carbon, with bond angles of about 120 degrees, because it has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
steps: The positive carbon in CH3CH2+ is bonded to three atoms (C, H, H).
It has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
Three electron domains repel to 120 degrees (trigonal planar).
The carbon is sp2 hybridised, so the ion is planar around C+.

questions.question: Draw a section of the polymer formed from methyl 2-methylpropenoate showing two repeat units.
steps: Monomer CH2=C(CH3)COOCH3 has one C=C.
The C=C opens; repeat unit -CH2-C(CH3)(COOCH3)-.
Join two units head to tail.
Result: -CH2-C(CH3)(COOCH3)-CH2-C(CH3)(COOCH3)-.

questions.question: Draw the molecular ion peaks for 2-chloropropane from the Cl isotopes (35Cl:37Cl = 3:1, Mr 78.5).
